classification.difficultyReason: Generalises the repeated-remainder explanation to bound the cycle length for any denominator.

content.prompt: Explain why the cycle length of a recurring decimal corresponding to a fraction is always less than the denominator of the fraction.

answer.short: For denominator $n$, there are only $n-1$ possible nonzero remainders. A repeated remainder starts the same digit sequence again, so the cycle length is at most $n-1$, which is less than $n$.
answer.worked: Let the denominator be $n$. In long division, the possible nonzero remainders are $1,2,\ldots,n-1$. A zero remainder would make the decimal terminate. Each remainder determines the next digit and the next remainder, so when a remainder repeats, the digit sequence repeats too. There are only $n-1$ nonzero remainders, so the recurring cycle has at most $n-1$ digits. Therefore its length is less than $n$.
